name: Battle of Ayacucho
info: On the Pampa de Ayacucho in the Peruvian highlands, Antonio José de Sucre's United Liberation Army defeated the royalist army of Viceroy José de la Serna, who was wounded and captured, and the royalists capitulated, ending Spanish rule in Peru.

facts.place: Pampa de Ayacucho (also called Quinua), a few kilometres from the town of Quinua and from Ayacucho, in the Peruvian highlands, Peru
facts.sides: The United Liberation Army under Marshal Antonio José de Sucre, and the royalist army of Peru under Viceroy José de la Serna, with Lieutenant General José de Canterac as chief of the high command. Troop numbers are debated: the armies began with 8,500 independentists and 9,310 royalists, and on the day there were perhaps 5,780 independentists and 6,906 royalists.
facts.outcome: The royalist army was broken, Viceroy La Serna was wounded and taken prisoner, and Canterac signed a capitulation with Sucre. Sucre gives independentist losses as 370 killed and 609 wounded, and royalist losses as about 1,800 dead and 700 wounded.

t: The royalists left a strong defensive position on high ground because they had food for less than five days and the Colombian reinforcements Bolívar expected would have made their position worse.
Troop numbers are debated: the armies began the campaign at 8,500 independentists and 9,310 royalists, but by the day of the battle there were perhaps 5,780 and 6,906.
The war in Peru ended with a capitulation, but fighting went on in Upper Peru until April 1825 and the siege of Callao lasted until 1826.
dyk: The Spanish historian Juan Carlos Losada has argued that the result had been agreed beforehand between commanders on both sides, a theory he admits can only be speculation because the main figures kept silent.
ev: A revolt led by Rafael Riego in Spain forces King Ferdinand VII to restore the liberal Constitution of 1812, and no reinforcements are sent to America
General José de la Serna overthrows Viceroy Pezuela in a coup at Aznapuquio
Troops at Callao mutiny and go over to the royalists, and Canterac occupies Lima
Bolívar faces Canterac at Junín, and in October gives Sucre command of the new front
The royalists inflict more than 500 casualties on Sucre's army at Corpahuaico
Sucre's army defeats the royalists at Ayacucho and the viceroy is captured
Olañeta is killed at Tumusla and royalist resistance in Upper Peru ends
The siege of the fortresses of Callao ends

sections.background:
In January 1820 a revolt in Spain, encouraged by General Rafael Riego, forced King Ferdinand VII to restore the liberal Spanish Constitution of 1812. An expedition of 20,000 soldiers meant for the Río de la Plata had joined the revolt, so Spain had no reinforcements to send to America, and the royalist armies of Peru and New Spain had to deal with the patriots on their own. In Peru, General José de la Serna overthrew Viceroy Joaquín de la Pezuela in a coup at Aznapuquio on 29 January 1821.

The royalists then won victories at Torata and Moquegua, in the Puno campaign that began with Zepita, and over Antonio José de Sucre's Gran Colombian force at Arequipa in October 1823. In February 1824 nearly two thousand men of the garrison at Callao mutinied and went over to the royalists, and José de Canterac occupied Lima.

Then the royalists divided. Ferdinand regained control in Spain, annulled La Serna's appointment as viceroy, and in early 1824 Pedro Antonio Olañeta led the royalist army of Upper Peru in revolt against the liberal viceroy. La Serna sent Jerónimo Valdés with 5,000 men against him. Simón Bolívar took advantage of the weakened royalist defences to face Canterac at Junín on 6 August 1824. On 7 October, with his troops before Cusco, he gave Sucre command of the new front and withdrew to Lima to find loans and to receive a Colombian division of 4,000 men under José Antonio Páez.
sections.forces:
The royalists had exhausted their resources in a marching war without winning a decisive victory, and both armies suffered disease and desertion in the harsh conditions of the Andes. The royalist commanders took position on the heights of Kunturkunka, a good defensive position that they could not hold for long, as they had food for less than five days. Colombian reinforcements were expected, which would mean certain defeat for them.

Debate exists over the numbers. The armies began with similar forces, 8,500 independentists and 9,310 royalists, but these dropped over the following weeks until, on the day of the battle, there were perhaps 5,780 independentists and 6,906 royalists.

The United Liberation Army was commanded by Marshal Sucre, with General Agustín Gamarra as chief of the high command and General William Miller commanding the cavalry. Its First Division under General José María Córdova had 2,300 men, its Second Division under General José de La Mar 1,580, and its reserve under General Jacinto Lara 1,700. The Colombian rifles battalion was composed largely of European troops, mostly British volunteers, but most of the foreign troops stayed in reserve.

The royalist army was led by Viceroy La Serna, with Lieutenant General Canterac as chief of the high command and Brigadier Valentín Ferraz commanding the cavalry. Its Vanguard Division under Jerónimo Valdés had 2,006 men, the First Division under Juan Antonio Monet 2,000, the Second under Alejandro González Villalobos 1,700, and the Reserve under José Carratalá 1,200.
sections.course:
On 3 December at Corpahuaico, also called Matará, the royalists cost Sucre's army more than 500 casualties and much of its ammunition and artillery, against 30 of their own. Sucre kept his army in orderly retreat.

Canterac's plan was for the vanguard division to cross the river Pampas and flank Sucre's left, while the rest of the royalist army came down frontally from the Condorcunca hill and charged the main body, which they expected to be disorganised. The royalists thus gave up their defensive ground and moved onto an exposed slope, unable to protect their movements. Córdova's division, supported by Miller's cavalry, fired on royalist troops that could not form battle lines as they descended.

Colonel Joaquín Rubín de Celis, who commanded the first royalist regiment and had to protect the mule-drawn artillery, moved carelessly onto the plain and was killed. Monet crossed the ravine without waiting for his cavalry and was surrounded; he was wounded and three of his commanders were killed. Ferraz's cavalry charged but suffered heavy casualties from confusion and crossfire. At the other end, the divisions of La Mar and Lara stopped the assault of Valdés's veterans.

Canterac led the reserve across the plain, but the Gerona battalions, which had lost almost all their veterans in Olañeta's rebellion, scattered before meeting the enemy, and the Ferdinand VII battalion followed after feeble resistance. By one o'clock the viceroy had been wounded and captured with many of his officers. Valdés was still fighting, but the battle was won by the independentists.
sections.aftermath:
According to Sucre, independentist casualties were 370 killed and 609 wounded, and the royalists lost about 1,800 dead and 700 wounded. Valdés retreated with the remnants of his division to a hill held by the rearguard, where he joined 200 cavalrymen gathered round Canterac and some scattered soldiers. Fleeing, demoralised men shot their own officers who were trying to regroup them. With the main body of the army broken and the viceroy a prisoner, the royalist leaders surrendered.

Because La Serna was seriously injured, Canterac negotiated the capitulation with Sucre. Under its principal terms the royalist army agreed to end hostilities, the remaining royalist soldiers were to stay in the fortresses of Callao, and the Peruvian republic was to pay the debt owed to the countries that had given military contributions to the independence movement.

The war did not end everywhere at once. Sucre entered Upper Peru on 25 February 1825. Olañeta, at Potosí, called a war council that agreed to continue resistance in the name of Ferdinand VII, but royalist units there rebelled one after another, and Colonel Medinacelli with 300 soldiers turned on him. Olañeta was killed at the Battle of Tumusla on 2 April 1825, and General José María Valdez surrendered on 7 April. The siege of the fortresses of Callao ended in 1826.
sections.sources:
The independentist side is known from Sucre's own report of the battle, which gives the order of the line and the casualty figures, and from the memoirs of General William Miller, a British officer who served with Bolívar. Miller and Sucre disagree on one point: Miller places the Junín Hussars in his cavalry division, Sucre does not. Sucre's report also does not mention the mounted grenadiers of the Río de la Plata, whom Miller lists.

The royalist side is described in the memoirs of the Spanish officer Andrés García Camba, published in 1846. Historians debate the number of troops on each side, and the figures for the day of the battle are put at 'perhaps' 5,780 and 6,906.

The rapid collapse of the royalists has also been explained as an agreement. Juan Carlos Losada calls the surrender the 'Ayacucho betrayal' and argues that the result had been settled between opposing commanders, with Monet responsible, so that the losers could keep their honour in defeat rather than be judged traitors for surrendering without a battle. He concedes that the main figures kept a pact of silence, so that this can only be speculation. The theory rests on the view that liberal-minded royalist commanders preferred an independentist victory to an absolutist Spain. García Camba records that officers returning to Spain, called 'ayacuchos', were accused of a 'Masonic defeat' and answered that it was lost 'in the way battles are lost'.
sections.legacy:
In Peru the battle is considered the end of the Spanish American wars of independence. It secured the independence of Peru and ensured that of the other South American states still fighting. Sucre's campaign continued through 1825 in Upper Peru, and the modern Peruvian Army celebrates the anniversary of the battle.

In Lima, Bolívar summoned the Congress of Panama on 7 December to unite the new independent countries, but only Gran Colombia ratified the project. Four years later Gran Colombia split into the countries that now exist in northern South America, owing to the personal ambitions of many of its generals and the lack of a shared vision of South America as one nation.

Upper Peru declared its independence on 6 August 1825, and the new state was named República Bolívar in honour of the Liberator, who declined the presidency and gave it to Sucre. A Potosí deputy, Manuel Martín Cruz, proposed that as Rome came from Romulus, Bolivia could come from Bolívar.

Sucre was made General in Chief of the Army of the Republic by the Congress of Colombia and Grand Marshal of Ayacucho by the Congress of Peru. In 1825 Bolívar published a short life of Sucre in which he called the battle the work of Sucre and wrote that its planning was perfect and its execution divine.

summary: At Ayacucho on 9 December 1824 Sucre's United Liberation Army defeated the royalist army of Viceroy La Serna, who was wounded and captured, and Canterac signed a capitulation. The battle is held in Peru to mark the end of the Spanish American wars of independence, though fighting continued in Upper Peru and at Callao.
notes: Troop numbers: the article gives 8,500 vs 9,310 at the start and 'perhaps' 5,780 vs 6,906 on the day. The independentist division strengths (2,300, 1,580, 1,700) add to 5,580, not 5,780; the royalist ones add to 6,906. I did not sum them in the text.
The article lists Carratalá's Reserve Division but the narrative has Canterac leading the reserve across the plain, and it calls Lara's force both Reserve and Third Division.
Garbled or odd: 'Boltijeros (sic)' in Sucre's quoted report; the Congress of Panama is dated 7 December in the article, before the battle.

Left out: Blanco Fombona's claim about Rivadavia and the Buenos Aires truce, the grenadier regiment's revolt at Lurin, Bolívar's reply 'Triumph!', Riva Agüero and Tagle, Olañeta's 60,000 pieces of gold, the Bolivian declaration's text.
The article's lead calls the battle decisive and says it ensured independence for the other belligerent South American states; I kept that as the Peruvian view in legacy.
The dyk and sources lean on Losada's theory, which the article presents as one historian's argument.
